title: Hosting a cabin rental in the Smokies: Gatlinburg, Pigeon Forge and Sevierville
summary: Smokies cabin rental permits for Gatlinburg, Pigeon Forge, Sevierville and Sevier County, taxes, seasons, and a cabin turnover checklist.
body_markdown:
[All posts](https://prohost.ai/blog)


**The Smokies are one of the biggest cabin-rental markets in the US, because the most visited national park in the country sits at the end of the road. Gatlinburg, Pigeon Forge and Sevierville each license rentals their own way, Sevier County added a fire-safety permit in 2024, and a cabin on a mountain road has operations a city condo never will: hot tubs, steep driveways, wildfire season and bears. This guide covers the permits, taxes, seasons and turnover work, with sources, as of November 19, 2026.**


## Key takeaways


- **Know whose rules you're under.** Gatlinburg, Pigeon Forge and Sevierville each have their own license or permit. Unincorporated Sevier County has required an annual permit and fire inspection since January 1, 2024 ([Sevier County](https://seviercountytn.gov/news_detail_T2_R68.php) ).
- **Airbnb collects most of the taxes, but not all.** It collects Tennessee sales tax and local occupancy taxes ([Airbnb Help Center](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2330) ). Gatlinburg's 1.25% gross receipts tax is on you ([City of Gatlinburg](https://cms9files1.revize.com/gatlinburg/Finance/New%20Business%20Overnight%20Rental.pdf) ).
- **Demand is enormous.** Great Smoky Mountains National Park had 11,527,939 visits in 2025, the most of any national park ([NPS](https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1207/03-13-26-2025-visitation-statsitics.htm) ).
- **October is the peak.** Leaf season and summer are the busy stretches. January and February are the slowest.
- **Cabins need a cabin checklist.** Hot tub chemistry, fireplaces and gas logs, winter driveways, pests and bears. A generic turnover list misses all of them.

## Where we're coming from


We host in Hawaii, the Smokies and Joshua Tree. The Smokies is the market where operations are most physical: more square footage, more amenities, more things that can break on a hill. Before ProhostAI I spent 6 years at Airbnb as a staff data scientist on the hosting team. The pattern in cabin markets is consistent: guests book for the amenities in the photos, and the reviews follow whether those amenities worked.


## Permits: which one applies to you


Your address decides your rules. Check whether the cabin is inside Gatlinburg, Pigeon Forge or Sevierville city limits, or in unincorporated Sevier County.


### Gatlinburg


The city's overnight rental sheet lists what a new rental needs ([City of Gatlinburg](https://cms9files1.revize.com/gatlinburg/Finance/New%20Business%20Overnight%20Rental.pdf) ):


- A **City of Gatlinburg business license** ($15) and a **Sevier County business license** ($15).
- A **Tennessee Department of Revenue** tax account.
- A **Gatlinburg Tourist Residency Permit.** Ask the city for the current fee and zoning rules for your address before you list.


### Pigeon Forge


Pigeon Forge licenses overnight rentals and limits them by zoning. Call the city's business license office with your parcel number before you buy or list, and ask which zones allow overnight rentals and whether a property in a residential zone is grandfathered.


### Sevierville


Sevierville has required an **annual short-term rental operational permit** since August 2021. The permit includes a Fire Department life-safety inspection, and you apply online through MGOconnect ([City of Sevierville](https://www.seviervilletn.org/467/Short-Term-Rentals) ).


### Unincorporated Sevier County


Since **January 1, 2024** , every short-term rental outside city limits needs an annual permit and an annual inspection by the Sevier County Fire Marshal's Office ([Sevier County](https://seviercountytn.gov/news_detail_T2_R68.php) ):


- **Fee:** $250 a year for a rental that sleeps 12 or fewer, plus $25 per occupant above 12.
- **Inspection:** smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, escape routes and electrical. The county recommends a fire extinguisher on each level.
- **Re-inspections:** the third and later ones carry a fee, so fix everything on the first list.

Two things to watch. First, the marketplace only remits for stays booked on that marketplace. Direct bookings and stays from a platform that doesn't collect are on you. Second, Gatlinburg's gross receipts tax is the owner's, and the city says marketplaces don't pay it ([city sheet](https://cms9files1.revize.com/gatlinburg/Finance/New%20Business%20Overnight%20Rental.pdf) ). Talk to a Tennessee preparer about your setup. This is a summary, not tax advice.


## Seasons and demand


- **The park drives the market.** 11,527,939 recreation visits in 2025, first among national parks ([NPS, March 13, 2026](https://www.nps.gov/orgs/1207/03-13-26-2025-visitation-statsitics.htm) ).
- **October is the busiest month** with leaf season, followed by summer. January and February are the slowest months in the park's monthly counts.
- **Winter is short and uneven.** Newfound Gap Road (US 441), the main road through the park, is open year-round but closes ahead of winter storms and for snow and ice ([NPS seasonal roads](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/planyourvisit/seasonalroads.htm) ). Several scenic roads, like Roaring Fork, close for the winter.
- **Parking tags:** since March 1, 2023, any car parked in the park for more than 15 minutes needs a Park It Forward tag. It was $5 a day, $15 a week or $40 a year at launch ([NPS](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/news/great-smoky-mountains-national-park-reminds-visitors-of-parking-tag-requirement.htm) ). Put that in your guidebook. It's one of the easy questions an AI can answer for you.


For pricing: book October and holiday weeks at the top of your range, use dynamic pricing ([PriceLabs](https://prohost.ai/integrations/pricelabs) or[Beyond](https://prohost.ai/integrations/beyond) ) for the rest of the year, and use[gap-night offers](https://prohost.ai/features/upsells) to fill the midweek nights between weekend stays in winter.


## Cabin operations


### Wildfire is part of the market's history


In November 2016, the Chimney Tops 2 fire burned about 11,000 acres in the park and spread into Gatlinburg ([NPS](https://www.nps.gov/grsm/learn/chimney-tops-2-fire.htm) ). For a host, that means three things: keep the county's smoke alarms and extinguishers current, keep brush and leaves cleared from around the cabin and deck, and have a written evacuation note in the guidebook with the route out and the county's emergency alert sign-up.


### Hot tubs


A hot tub is a top amenity in cabin listings and a common source of complaints. The water chemistry and cover condition are the cleaner's job on every turnover, and the drain-and-refill schedule depends on use. Put a hot tub section on the turnover checklist and require a photo.


### Fireplaces and gas logs


Guests want them on and don't know how they work. Post the steps in the guidebook and on a card next to the unit, and include them in the check-in message for winter stays.


### Driveways and roads


Many cabins sit on steep mountain roads. In winter, ice and snow can make a driveway unsafe for a two-wheel-drive car. Say so in the listing, tell guests in the pre-arrival message when the forecast calls for ice, and know who plows or salts your road.


### Bears and pests


Bears are a feature of the Smokies, and so are bear-proof trash rules. Tell guests where the trash goes and when, every stay. Ladybugs, stink bugs and mice come indoors in the fall. Pest control on a schedule is cheaper than a one-star review.


## A cabin turnover checklist you can copy


```text
SMOKIES CABIN TURNOVER CHECKLIST


Arrival readiness
[ ] Door code works (test keypad); backup code noted
[ ] Driveway clear; if ice is forecast, salt/sand on hand and guest warned
[ ] Porch and deck lights work


Hot tub
[ ] Test and balance water (sanitizer, pH); log the reading
[ ] Clean filter if due; check water level
[ ] Cover clean, intact, straps locked
[ ] Photo of clear water + cover on


Fireplace / gas logs
[ ] Off and cool; glass clean
[ ] Remote has batteries; instructions card in place
[ ] Firewood stocked if provided


Safety (Sevier County inspection items)
[ ] Smoke and CO alarms tested
[ ] Fire extinguisher on each level, gauge in green
[ ] Escape routes clear; windows open


Outside
[ ] Trash in bear-proof cans; pickup day noted for guest
[ ] Leaves and debris cleared from deck and near the cabin
[ ] Grill clean, propane level checked


Inside
[ ] Standard clean: linens, towels, kitchen, bathrooms
[ ] Pest check: windowsills, under sinks, attic access
[ ] Games, movies, arcade or pool table: all pieces, all working
[ ] Thermostat set to arrival temperature
[ ] Guidebook current: parking tag, roads, trash, hot tub rules


```

## FAQ


**Do I need a permit for a cabin outside city limits?** Yes. Since January 1, 2024, unincorporated Sevier County requires an annual permit and fire inspection ([Sevier County](https://seviercountytn.gov/news_detail_T2_R68.php) ).


**Does Airbnb collect Tennessee taxes?** Airbnb collects Tennessee sales tax and local occupancy taxes on stays booked through Airbnb ([article 2330](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2330) ). Gatlinburg's 1.25% gross receipts tax is the owner's.


**When is peak season in the Smokies?** October, then summer. January and February are the slowest months.


**Do guests need a parking tag for the national park?** Yes, for any stop over 15 minutes, since March 1, 2023. Driving through doesn't need one.


**Should I mention a steep driveway in the listing?** Yes. Say it in the listing, and again in the pre-arrival message when ice is forecast. A guest who knew beforehand plans for it. A guest who finds out at 9 p.m. in a sedan writes about it.


## The takeaway


The Smokies have the demand. What separates a good cabin from an average one is the operation: the right permit for your address, taxes you know you owe, and a turnover that checks the hot tub, the fireplace, the driveway and the trash every time. Write the checklist once, require the photos, and let software schedule the rest.
